reading.ours: two units of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — an instrument check, and it is printed first because nothing below it means anything until it passes. The true ratio is a little UNDER 2: both sides pay the driving loop once, so the exact expectation is (2u + L) / (u + L) with L the loop and u one unit, which at sixteen dependent steps per unit puts it around 1.9. A reading below 1.5 means this process could not resolve a deliberate doubling, and the runner voids the report rather than printing prices under it.

reading.ours: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: the same body again, over its own copy of the same state
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — the noise floor. The two sides are identical code over identical, separately-allocated state, so the true ratio is 1.00 exactly and every departure from it printed here was produced by this machine at this moment. The rule that follows is the one the whole table is read under: NO RATIO CLOSER TO 1.00 THAN THIS GAP IS A READING. It also bounds the per-row noise figure, which is the same idea measured again inside every pair — each pair times its floor twice, once before our side and once after, and prints how far the two disagreed.

reading.ours: collection.find(id) — the identity of a key, or nothing
reading.caveat: THE CALIBRATION ROW. `find` is one call into the identity store and one `Map.get`, so if this reads much above 1 the instrument is measuring call overhead rather than the library, and every other ratio in this table should be read with that in mind. Every key hits — a miss is a different path on both sides and would mix two prices. What ours hands back is an identity and not a row: a caller still has to read `.entity` off it, which the row below prices separately.

reading.ours: collection.slotOf(id) — resolve a key to an identity, minting on a miss
reading.caveat: THE FLOOR CANNOT MINT, and that is the whole difference: `slotOf` promises an identity for a key the population has never seen, so a caller can subscribe to a row before it arrives. Every key here HITS, so the minting branch never runs — what is left is the map read plus the closure `slotOf` allocates to pass the mint function, on every call, hit or miss. Direction: inflates our ratio by exactly that allocation, and it is a real cost a caller pays. Read this against `find.vs-map-get` directly above: the gap between the two is what the mint-on-miss promise costs on the hit path.

reading.ours: slot.entity — the row behind an identity you already hold
reading.caveat: ONE INDIRECTION AGAINST NONE, which is the smallest thing this table can ask about and is close to the resolution floor — read it against the control rows before treating any part of it as a result. Ours answers `TPriceDataRow | undefined` because an identity may carry no value; the floor answers a row. This body does NOT narrow the undefined, so the branch a real consumer writes is charged to neither side.

reading.ours: groupBy(collection, ['group'])('group-7') — resolve a group to a live handle
reading.caveat: THE MOST UNEQUAL PAIR IN THIS SUITE, and it is on the table because the engine's own documentation says "resolved ONCE — hold it", so the row is what IGNORING that advice costs. Ours resolves the bucket, takes a hold on it so the frame sweep cannot drop it underneath the caller, and builds an observable — a getter closure, a subscribe closure, a detach closure and the object they hang on. Five allocations against a hash. The floor hands back a container that can be iterated and cannot be subscribed to, cannot be handed to `db.computed`, and will be the WRONG container the moment somebody rebuilds it. Direction: inflates our ratio enormously, and it is a real number for anybody who writes this inside a render body. This body never calls `detach()`, so the hold count grows and is never given back — that is one decrement we do not charge ourselves for.
